claim: SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in over 6 million deaths worldwide since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020.
source: SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in over 6 million deaths worldwide since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 (G. W. H. Organization, 2023; C. for S. Science, E, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to external sources (G. W. H. Organization, 2023; C. for S. Science, E, 2023).

claim: The development of mRNA and other vaccines has played a large and critical role in reducing mortality since their introduction in 2021.
source: The development of mRNA and other vaccines has played a large and critical role in reducing mortality since their introduction in 2021 (Suthar et al., 2022; Rahmani et al., 2022; Watson et al., 2022; Mohammed et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Suthar et al., 2022; Rahmani et al., 2022; Watson et al., 2022; Mohammed et al., 2022).

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro or Nsp5) is a well-studied antiviral drug target because its activity is essential for viral replication.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro or Nsp5) is a well-studied antiviral drug target because its activity is essential for viral replication.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.

claim: More than 600 Mpro crystal structures are currently available in the protein databank.
source: More than 600 Mpro crystal structures – the majority with bound small molecule inhibitors – are currently available in the protein databank (Burley et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Burley et al., 2021.

claim: Mpro is necessary for the proteolysis of 11 different cleavage sites in the two SARS-CoV-2 extended viral polypeptides.
source: Mpro is necessary for the proteolysis of 11 different cleavage sites in the two SARS-CoV-2 extended viral polypeptides, which results in the liberation of mature non-structural proteins that are essential for host infection and viral propagation (Wilamowski et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Thoms et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Wilamowski et al., 2021; Yan et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Thoms et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020).

claim: Approximately 20 structures of Mpro in complex with different viral cleavage sequences have been determined.
source: Approximately 20 structures of Mpro in complex with different viral cleavage sequences have been determined (MacDonald et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022; Shaqra et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations (MacDonald et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022; Shaqra et al., 2022).

claim: Gordon et al. expressed tagged SARS-CoV-2 proteins in human embryonic kidney cells (HEK293T/17) and employed affinity purification mass spectrometry (AP-MS) to map proteome-wide virus-host protein interactions.
source: Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, Gordon et al. expressed tagged SARS-CoV-2 proteins in human embryonic kidney cells (HEK293T/17) and employed affinity purification mass spectrometry (AP-MS) to map proteome-wide virus-host protein interactions, in which a putative interaction between catalytically inactive SARS-CoV-2 Mpro (Cys145Ala) and the human tRNA methyltransferase TRMT1 was identified (Gordon et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2020b.

claim: A putative interaction between catalytically inactive SARS-CoV-2 Mpro (Cys145Ala) and the human tRNA methyltransferase TRMT1 was identified by AP-MS.
source: Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, Gordon et al. expressed tagged SARS-CoV-2 proteins in human embryonic kidney cells (HEK293T/17) and employed affinity purification mass spectrometry (AP-MS) to map proteome-wide virus-host protein interactions, in which a putative interaction between catalytically inactive SARS-CoV-2 Mpro (Cys145Ala) and the human tRNA methyltransferase TRMT1 was identified (Gordon et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2020b.

claim: AP-MS experiments with wild-type (WT) Mpro found no stable interaction with TRMT1.
source: Analogous AP-MS experiments with wild-type (WT) Mpro found no stable interaction with TRMT1, and subsequent mapping with SARS-CoV-1 proteins also found a TRMT1 interaction exclusively with Cys145Ala Mpro, suggesting that coronavirus Mpro may recognize and actively cleave human TRMT1 in cells (Gordon et al., 2020b; Gordon et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon et al., 2020b; Gordon et al., 2020a.

claim: Coronavirus Mpro may recognize and actively cleave human TRMT1 in cells.
source: Analogous AP-MS experiments with wild-type (WT) Mpro found no stable interaction with TRMT1, and subsequent mapping with SARS-CoV-1 proteins also found a TRMT1 interaction exclusively with Cys145Ala Mpro, suggesting that coronavirus Mpro may recognize and actively cleave human TRMT1 in cells (Gordon et al., 2020b; Gordon et al., 2020a).
evidence: Inference based on AP-MS data cited from Gordon et al., 2020b; Gordon et al., 2020a.

claim: TRMT1 is a tRNA-modifying enzyme responsible for installing N2,N2-dimethylguanosine (m2,2G).
source: TRMT1 is a tRNA-modifying enzyme responsible for installing N2,N2-dimethylguanosine (m2,2G), an abundant tRNA modification found at the G26 position of human tRNAs (Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chou et al., 2017.

claim: m2,2G is an abundant tRNA modification found at the G26 position of human tRNAs.
source: TRMT1 is a tRNA-modifying enzyme responsible for installing N2,N2-dimethylguanosine (m2,2G), an abundant tRNA modification found at the G26 position of human tRNAs (Chou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chou et al., 2017.

claim: Human HEK293T cells lacking TRMT1 have significantly decreased global protein synthesis and reduced proliferation.
source: Human HEK293T cells lacking TRMT1, and therefore the m2,2G26 modification, have significantly decreased global protein synthesis and reduced proliferation (Dewe et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dewe et al., 2017.

claim: Human neural stem cells with TRMT1 knockdowns have hypersensitivity to redox stress.
source: Human neural stem cells with TRMT1 knockdowns were found to have hypersensitivity to redox stress, implicating TRMT1 and the m2,2G26 modification in the regulation of redox homeostasis (Dewe et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dewe et al., 2017.

claim: TRMT1 and the m2,2G26 modification are implicated in the regulation of redox homeostasis.
source: Human neural stem cells with TRMT1 knockdowns were found to have hypersensitivity to redox stress, implicating TRMT1 and the m2,2G26 modification in the regulation of redox homeostasis (Dewe et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on data cited from Dewe et al., 2017.

claim: TRMT1 contains a peptide sequence (527–534) consistent with the cleavage consensus for Mpro.
source: TRMT1 contains a peptide sequence (527–534) consistent with the cleavage consensus for Mpro, located in an AlphaFold2-predicted (Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021) surface-exposed region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) linking the TRMT1 N-terminal SAM-dependent methyltransferase domain and the C-terminal zinc finger domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and AlphaFold2 prediction cited from Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021, and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TRMT1 (527–534) sequence is located in a surface-exposed region linking the TRMT1 N-terminal SAM-dependent methyltransferase domain and the C-terminal zinc finger domain.
source: TRMT1 contains a peptide sequence (527–534) consistent with the cleavage consensus for Mpro, located in an AlphaFold2-predicted (Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021) surface-exposed region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) linking the TRMT1 N-terminal SAM-dependent methyltransferase domain and the C-terminal zinc finger domain (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by AlphaFold2 prediction cited from Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021, and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 Mpro-directed cleavage of TRMT1 could have direct impacts on both host and viral protein synthesis.
source: SARS-CoV-2 Mpro-directed cleavage of TRMT1, and subsequent downregulation of tRNA m2,2G26 modification during infection, could therefore have direct impacts on both host and viral protein synthesis, as well as phenotypes linked to redox stress.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on known functions of TRMT1.

claim: The TRMT1 cleavage site is highly conserved in mammals, except in Muroidea, where TRMT1 is likely resistant to cleavage.
source: Evolutionary analysis shows the TRMT1 cleavage site is highly conserved in mammals, except in Muroidea, where TRMT1 is likely resistant to cleavage.
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis data shown in the manuscript (Figure 6).

claim: TRMT1 proteolysis results in reduced tRNA binding.
source: TRMT1 proteolysis results in reduced tRNA binding and elimination of tRNA methyltransferase activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript (Figure 2D).

claim: TRMT1 proteolysis results in elimination of tRNA methyltransferase activity.
source: TRMT1 proteolysis results in reduced tRNA binding and elimination of tRNA methyltransferase activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript (Figure 2C).

claim: The structure of an Mpro-TRMT1 peptide complex shows how TRMT1 engages the Mpro active site in an uncommon substrate binding conformation.
source: We also determined the structure of an Mpro-TRMT1 peptide complex that shows how TRMT1 engages the Mpro active site in an uncommon substrate binding conformation.
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in the manuscript (Figure 3, Figure 4).

claim: Kinetic discrimination occurs during a later step of Mpro-mediated proteolysis following substrate binding.
source: Finally, enzymology and molecular dynamics simulations indicate that kinetic discrimination occurs during a later step of Mpro-mediated proteolysis following substrate binding.
evidence: Supported by kinetic data and MD simulations shown in the manuscript (Figure 5, Figure 7).

claim: Proteolysis of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection impairs both TRMT1 tRNA binding and tRNA modification activity.
source: Together, these data provide new insights into substrate recognition by SARS-CoV-2 Mpro that could help guide future antiviral therapeutic development and show how proteolysis of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection impairs both TRMT1 tRNA binding and tRNA modification activity to disrupt host translation and potentially impact COVID-19 pathogenesis or phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript (Figure 2C, 2D).

claim: Proteolysis of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection may disrupt host translation.
source: Together, these data provide new insights into substrate recognition by SARS-CoV-2 Mpro that could help guide future antiviral therapeutic development and show how proteolysis of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection impairs both TRMT1 tRNA binding and tRNA modification activity to disrupt host translation and potentially impact COVID-19 pathogenesis or phenotypes.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on experimental data.

claim: Proteolysis of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection may potentially impact COVID-19 pathogenesis or phenotypes.
source: Together, these data provide new insights into substrate recognition by SARS-CoV-2 Mpro that could help guide future antiviral therapeutic development and show how proteolysis of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection impairs both TRMT1 tRNA binding and tRNA modification activity to disrupt host translation and potentially impact COVID-19 pathogenesis or phenotypes.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on experimental data.

claim: Full-length TRMT1 was incubated with either catalytically inactive Mpro Cys145Ala or active WT Mpro.
source: TRMT1 was incubated with either catalytically inactive Mpro Cys145Ala or active WT Mpro, and TRMT1 cleavage was monitored by western blot using two TRMT1-specific polyclonal antibodies: a dual-domain recognizing antibody specific for portions of both the methyltransferase and zinc finger domain (anti-TRMT1 460–659), and a single-domain recognizing antibody specific for only the zinc finger domain (anti-TRMT1 609–659).
evidence: Describes experimental procedure.

claim: FL TRMT1 was stable during a 2 hr incubation with inactive Cys145Ala Mpro.
source: As expected, FL TRMT1 (~75 kDa) was stable during a 2 hr incubation with inactive Cys145Ala Mpro.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When incubated with WT Mpro, the intensity of the band corresponding to FL TRMT1 was reduced by >90% after 2 hr.
source: However, when incubated with WT Mpro, the intensity of the band corresponding to FL TRMT1, as measured by both TRMT1 antibodies, was reduced by >90% after 2 hr.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In western blots with cleaved TRMT1, the dual domain-recognizing anti-TRMT1(460–659) antibody showed the appearance of two new lower molecular weight bands.
source: In western blots with cleaved TRMT1, the dual domain-recognizing anti-TRMT1(460–659) antibody showed the appearance of two new lower molecular weight bands, corresponding to the anticipated molecular weights of the Mpro-mediated TRMT1 cleavage products (~61 kDa TRMT1 methyltransferase domain and ~14 kDa TRMT1 zinc finger domain).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The two new lower molecular weight bands correspond to the anticipated molecular weights of the Mpro-mediated TRMT1 cleavage products (~61 kDa TRMT1 methyltransferase domain and ~14 kDa TRMT1 zinc finger domain).
source: In western blots with cleaved TRMT1, the dual domain-recognizing anti-TRMT1(460–659) antibody showed the appearance of two new lower molecular weight bands, corresponding to the anticipated molecular weights of the Mpro-mediated TRMT1 cleavage products (~61 kDa TRMT1 methyltransferase domain and ~14 kDa TRMT1 zinc finger domain).
evidence: Inference based on observed molecular weights in western blot data (Figure 2A).

claim: HEK293T cell lysate was incubated with either Cys145Ala or WT Mpro, and endogenous TRMT1 levels were monitored over time by western blot.
source: HEK293T cell lysate was incubated with either Cys145Ala or WT Mpro, and endogenous TRMT1 levels were monitored over time by western blot (Figure 2B).
evidence: Describes experimental procedure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Incubation with Cys145Ala Mpro resulted in no change to the FL TRMT1 band over the course of 2 hr.
source: Incubation with Cys145Ala Mpro resulted in no change to the FL TRMT1 band over the course of 2 hr, while incubation with WT Mpro resulted in time-dependent proteolysis of FL TRMT1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Incubation with WT Mpro resulted in time-dependent proteolysis of FL TRMT1.
source: Incubation with Cys145Ala Mpro resulted in no change to the FL TRMT1 band over the course of 2 hr, while incubation with WT Mpro resulted in time-dependent proteolysis of FL TRMT1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: No build-up of cleavage products was observed during Mpro-mediated proteolysis of endogenous TRMT1.
source: Unlike in cleavage assays with recombinant TRMT1, no build-up of cleavage products was observed during Mpro-mediated proteolysis of endogenous TRMT1, suggesting instability and rapid degradation of cleaved TRMT1 fragments in human cell lysate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cleaved TRMT1 fragments are unstable and rapidly degraded in human cell lysate.
source: Unlike in cleavage assays with recombinant TRMT1, no build-up of cleavage products was observed during Mpro-mediated proteolysis of endogenous TRMT1, suggesting instability and rapid degradation of cleaved TRMT1 fragments in human cell lysate.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observation in Figure 2B.

claim: Both recombinant FL TRMT1 and endogenous FL TRMT1 in human cell lysate are viable substrates for cleavage by SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that both recombinant FL TRMT1 and endogenous FL TRMT1 in human cell lysate are viable substrates for cleavage by SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.
evidence: Conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Cleaved TRMT1 generated by incubation with Mpro WT exhibits a total loss of measurable tRNA methyltransferase activity.
source: Cleaved TRMT1 generated by incubation with Mpro WT exhibits a total loss of measurable tRNA methyltransferase activity, compared to TRMT1 incubated with Mpro Cys145Ala, which retains full activity comparable to TRMT1 alone (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TRMT1 incubated with Mpro Cys145Ala retains full tRNA methyltransferase activity comparable to TRMT1 alone.
source: Cleaved TRMT1 generated by incubation with Mpro WT exhibits a total loss of measurable tRNA methyltransferase activity, compared to TRMT1 incubated with Mpro Cys145Ala, which retains full activity comparable to TRMT1 alone (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mpro-cleaved TRMT1 has reduced affinity for tRNA.
source: Similarly, we found that Mpro-cleaved TRMT1 also had reduced affinity for tRNA, whereas TRMT1 incubated with Mpro Cys145Ala had comparable tRNA binding affinity to TRMT1 alone (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: TRMT1 incubated with Mpro Cys145Ala had comparable tRNA binding affinity to TRMT1 alone.
source: Similarly, we found that Mpro-cleaved TRMT1 also had reduced affinity for tRNA, whereas TRMT1 incubated with Mpro Cys145Ala had comparable tRNA binding affinity to TRMT1 alone (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cleaved TRMT1-tRNA complexes migrate at significantly higher apparent molecular weights as compared to uncleaved TRMT1-tRNA complexes.
source: While cleaved TRMT1 still retained some affinity for tRNA, we observed in EMSA experiments that cleaved TRMT1-tRNA complexes migrate at significantly higher apparent molecular weights as compared to uncleaved TRMT1-tRNA complexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TRMT1 cleavage products in vitro may form oligomers that have reduced affinity for tRNA.
source: This suggests that the TRMT1 cleavage products in vitro may form oligomers that have reduced affinity for tRNA, but based on the methyltransferase activity assays above, these oligomeric TRMT1-tRNA complexes cannot efficiently methylate bound tRNA.
evidence: Inference based on EMSA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Oligomeric TRMT1-tRNA complexes cannot efficiently methylate bound tRNA.
source: This suggests that the TRMT1 cleavage products in vitro may form oligomers that have reduced affinity for tRNA, but based on the methyltransferase activity assays above, these oligomeric TRMT1-tRNA complexes cannot efficiently methylate bound tRNA.
evidence: Inference based on methyltransferase activity data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Truncated TRMT1 constructs lacking the zinc finger domain have reduced tRNA modification activity in cells.
source: These observations are consistent with other studies that have shown truncated TRMT1 constructs lacking the zinc finger domain have reduced tRNA modification activity in cells (Dewe et al., 2017) or in vitro (Lu and Zhou, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dewe et al., 2017 and Lu and Zhou, 2023.

claim: Truncated TRMT1 constructs lacking the zinc finger domain have reduced tRNA modification activity in vitro.
source: These observations are consistent with other studies that have shown truncated TRMT1 constructs lacking the zinc finger domain have reduced tRNA modification activity in cells (Dewe et al., 2017) or in vitro (Lu and Zhou, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu and Zhou, 2023.

claim: Mpro-mediated cleavage of TRMT1 reduces its substrate tRNA binding affinity.
source: Together, our in vitro tRNA binding and modification assays directly show that Mpro-mediated cleavage of TRMT1 reduces its substrate tRNA binding affinity and completely incapacitates its tRNA m2,2G modification catalysis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mpro-mediated cleavage of TRMT1 completely incapacitates its tRNA m2,2G modification catalysis.
source: Together, our in vitro tRNA binding and modification assays directly show that Mpro-mediated cleavage of TRMT1 reduces its substrate tRNA binding affinity and completely incapacitates its tRNA m2,2G modification catalysis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The co-crystal structure of catalytically inactive Cys145Ala mutant Mpro in complex with the TRMT1 peptide sequence corresponding to the expected cleavage site, human TRMT1 residues 526–536, was determined at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: To visualize how TRMT1 is recognized and cleaved by the viral protease active site, we determined the co-crystal structure of catalytically inactive Cys145Ala mutant Mpro in complex with the TRMT1 peptide sequence corresponding to the expected cleavage site, human TRMT1 residues 526–536 (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1). The 1.9 Å resolution structure shows clear density for the TRMT1 peptide bound to the active site in one protomer of the Mpro dimer (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1.

claim: TRMT1 Gln530 occupies the critical S1 subsite pocket in the Mpro active site.
source: As expected based on alignment with the Mpro consensus cleavage sequence, TRMT1 Gln530 occupies the critical S1 subsite pocket in the Mpro active site (Figure 3A), positioning the Gln530-Ala531 peptide bond directly adjacent to the His41/Cys145 catalytic dyad for proteolytic cleavage (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Gln530-Ala531 peptide bond is positioned directly adjacent to the His41/Cys145 catalytic dyad for proteolytic cleavage.
source: As expected based on alignment with the Mpro consensus cleavage sequence, TRMT1 Gln530 occupies the critical S1 subsite pocket in the Mpro active site (Figure 3A), positioning the Gln530-Ala531 peptide bond directly adjacent to the His41/Cys145 catalytic dyad for proteolytic cleavage (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TRMT1 Leu529 corresponds to substrate position P2 and occupies the hydrophobic Mpro S2 pocket.
source: TRMT1 Leu529 corresponds to substrate position P2 and occupies the hydrophobic Mpro S2 pocket (Figure 3A), packing against Mpro residues His41, Met49, Met165, and Gln189 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: P3′ substrate residue TRMT1 Phe533 occupies the Mpro S3′ pocket.
source: P3′ substrate residue TRMT1 Phe533 occupies the Mpro S3′ pocket (Figure 3A), which is composed by Mpro residues His41, Cys44, Met49, and the backbone of Thr45 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Mpro S3′ pocket is composed by Mpro residues His41, Cys44, Met49, and the backbone of Thr45.
source: P3′ substrate residue TRMT1 Phe533 occupies the Mpro S3′ pocket (Figure 3A), which is composed by Mpro residues His41, Cys44, Met49, and the backbone of Thr45 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TRMT1 peptide binding to Mpro is mediated by numerous key sidechain and mainchain hydrogen bonding contacts.
source: TRMT1 peptide binding to Mpro is also mediated by numerous key sidechain and mainchain hydrogen bonding contacts (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The TRMT1 P1 Gln530 sidechain is specifically recognized by hydrogen bonding interactions with Mpro residues Phe140 and His163.
source: The TRMT1 P1 Gln530 sidechain is specifically recognized by hydrogen bonding interactions with Mpro residues Phe140 (Figure 3C) and His163 (Figure 3D), consistent with previous structures of Mpro bound to viral peptide substrates (Shaqra et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3C and 3D, and citation to Shaqra et al., 2022.

claim: The TRMT1 P2′ Asn532 sidechain interacts with Mpro Asn142.
source: Additionally, the TRMT1 P2′ Asn532 sidechain interacts with Mpro Asn142 (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A number of TRMT1 peptide backbone atoms make hydrogen bond contacts with Mpro surface residues.
source: A number of TRMT1 peptide backbone atoms (from TRMT1 residues Arg528, Leu529, Gln530, Asn532, and Thr534) make hydrogen bond contacts with Mpro surface residues (Mpro Gly143, Glu166, and Gln189 contacts shown in Figure 3C; Mpro Thr24, Thr26, Cys145Ala, and His164 contacts shown in Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The identified Mpro-targeted residues in human TRMT1 are conserved in the human population.
source: The identified Mpro-targeted residues in human TRMT1 are conserved in the human population (i.e. no missense polymorphisms), showing that human TRMT1 can be recognized and cleaved by SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.
evidence: Inference based on sequence conservation data.

claim: Human TRMT1 can be recognized and cleaved by SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.
source: The identified Mpro-targeted residues in human TRMT1 are conserved in the human population (i.e. no missense polymorphisms), showing that human TRMT1 can be recognized and cleaved by SARS-CoV-2 Mpro.
evidence: Conclusion based on sequence conservation and experimental data.

claim: Both TRMT1 and viral peptide backbones have nearly identical conformations for the N-terminal P4 → P1′ residues.
source: Analysis of aligned peptide substrates in the Mpro active site shows that both TRMT1 and viral peptide backbones have nearly identical conformations for the N-terminal P4 → P1′ residues.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Backbone geometries of C-terminal peptide residues (P2′ → P4′) diverge more significantly and fall into two distinct binding modes distinguished primarily by the P2′ Ψ dihedral angle.
source: In contrast, backbone geometries of C-terminal peptide residues (P2′ → P4′) diverge more significantly and fall into two distinct binding modes distinguished primarily by the P2′ Ψ dihedral angle (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The majority of viral peptide substrates adopt a binding conformation with P2′ Ψ≥157° in which the P3′ sidechain is positioned away from the Mpro surface ('P3′-out' conformation).
source: The majority of viral peptide substrates adopt a binding conformation with P2′ Ψ≥157 ° in which the P3′ sidechain is positioned away from the Mpro surface (Figure 4D), which we have designated as the 'P3′-out' conformation.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: TRMT1 and nsp6/7 bind in a distinct conformation with P2′ Ψ≤116° in which the P3′ sidechain is positioned toward the Mpro surface where it displaces Mpro Met49 to open and occupy pocket S3′ ('P3′-in' conformation).
source: In contrast, TRMT1 and a single viral peptide substrate, nsp6/7, bind in a distinct conformation with P2′ Ψ≤116 ° (Figure 4C) in which the P3′ sidechain (Phe in TRMT1, Met in nsp6/7) is positioned toward the Mpro surface where it displaces Mpro Met49 to open and occupy pocket S3′ (Figure 4D). We have designated this uncommon binding mode as the 'P3′-in' conformation.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The TRMT1 peptide is cleaved noticeably slower than the nsp4/5 N-terminal auto-processing sequence.
source: The TRMT1 peptide is cleaved noticeably slower than the nsp4/5 N-terminal auto-processing sequence (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1), with an approximately 200-fold decrease in kcat, 4-fold decrease in KM, and 50-fold decrease in catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) compared to Mpro-mediated cleavage of the nsp4/5 peptide (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: TRMT1 peptide cleavage has an approximately 200-fold decrease in kcat compared to nsp4/5 peptide cleavage.
source: The TRMT1 peptide is cleaved noticeably slower than the nsp4/5 N-terminal auto-processing sequence (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1), with an approximately 200-fold decrease in kcat, 4-fold decrease in KM, and 50-fold decrease in catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) compared to Mpro-mediated cleavage of the nsp4/5 peptide (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: TRMT1 peptide cleavage has a 4-fold decrease in KM compared to nsp4/5 peptide cleavage.
source: The TRMT1 peptide is cleaved noticeably slower than the nsp4/5 N-terminal auto-processing sequence (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1), with an approximately 200-fold decrease in kcat, 4-fold decrease in KM, and 50-fold decrease in catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) compared to Mpro-mediated cleavage of the nsp4/5 peptide (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: TRMT1 peptide cleavage has a 50-fold decrease in catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) compared to nsp4/5 peptide cleavage.
source: The TRMT1 peptide is cleaved noticeably slower than the nsp4/5 N-terminal auto-processing sequence (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1), with an approximately 200-fold decrease in kcat, 4-fold decrease in KM, and 50-fold decrease in catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) compared to Mpro-mediated cleavage of the nsp4/5 peptide (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: TRMT1 is cleaved with very comparable kinetics to the viral nsp8/9 cleavage sequence, with kcat, KM, and kcat/KM values all within ~3-fold.
source: However, TRMT1 is cleaved with very comparable kinetics to the viral nsp8/9 cleavage sequence, with kcat, KM, and kcat/KM values all within ~3-fold for TRMT1 vs nsp8/9 peptide cleavage.
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: TRMT1 (526–536) is a viable substrate for Mpro-targeted proteolysis.
source: These kinetic experiments show that, while the TRMT1 Mpro target sequence is cleaved less efficiently than the canonical nsp4/5 auto-processing site, the TRMT1 sequence is cleaved with kinetics very similar to the known nsp8/9 Mpro cleavage site in the viral polypeptide. This suggests that TRMT1 (526–536) is a viable substrate for Mpro-targeted proteolysis.
evidence: Conclusion based on kinetic data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the TRMT1-bound structure, Mpro Met49 is shifted to accommodate TRMT1 P3′ substrate residue Phe533 binding in the S3′ pocket.
source: In the TRMT1-bound structure, Mpro Met49 is shifted to accommodate TRMT1 P3′ substrate residue Phe533 binding in the S3′ pocket, and the Mpro Asn142 and Gln189 sidechains are repositioned to form hydrogen bonds with the TRMT1 peptide backbone.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Mpro Asn142 and Gln189 sidechains are repositioned to form hydrogen bonds with the TRMT1 peptide backbone.
source: In the TRMT1-bound structure, Mpro Met49 is shifted to accommodate TRMT1 P3′ substrate residue Phe533 binding in the S3′ pocket, and the Mpro Asn142 and Gln189 sidechains are repositioned to form hydrogen bonds with the TRMT1 peptide backbone.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No substantial changes in proteolysis kinetics were observed for cleavage of either nsp4/5 or TRMT1 substrates with any of the tested Mpro mutants (Met49Ala, Asn142Ala, Gln189Ala) or the TRMT1 Ala531Ser mutant peptide.
source: Surprisingly, we saw no substantial changes in proteolysis kinetics for cleavage of either nsp4/5 or TRMT1 substrates with any of the tested Mpro mutants (Met49Ala, Asn142Ala, Gln189Ala) or the TRMT1 Ala531Ser mutant peptide (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: None of the tested Mpro residues (Met49, Asn142, Gln189) alone play a significant role in determining differential cleavage rates for TRMT1 vs nsp4/5.
source: Surprisingly, we saw no substantial changes in proteolysis kinetics for cleavage of either nsp4/5 or TRMT1 substrates with any of the tested Mpro mutants (Met49Ala, Asn142Ala, Gln189Ala) or the TRMT1 Ala531Ser mutant peptide (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting none of these residues alone play a significant role in determining differential cleavage rates for TRMT1 vs nsp4/5.
evidence: Inference based on kinetic data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Mpro-mediated TRMT1 (526–536) cleavage sequence is highly conserved in primates.
source: Through comprehensive analyses, we identified rapidly evolving sites at the N- and C-termini of primate TRMT1, but we did not find any evidence of sites under positive selection at the Mpro-mediated TRMT1 (526–536) cleavage sequence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, Figure 6—source data 1). In fact, this sequence is highly conserved in primates (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Mpro cleavage site of TRMT1 (residues 526–536) is highly conserved in most mammals, including in bats that are the reservoir of SARS-CoVs.
source: A TRMT1 sequence analysis at the mammalian level further showed that the Mpro cleavage site of TRMT1 (residues 526–536) is highly conserved in most mammals, including in bats that are the reservoir of SARS-CoVs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In rodents, there has been a Q to K substitution fixed in all Muroidea at the TRMT1 cleavage site.
source: However, one exception is in rodents, where there has been a Q to K substitution fixed in all Muroidea (mouse, rat, hamster, etc.) (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: TRMT1 Gln530Lys was resistant to Mpro cleavage.
source: To test the impact of this substitution on Mpro-mediated cleavage, we generated a TRMT1 Gln530Lys mutant and incubated it with Mpro WT for a period of 2 hr (Figure 6D). We found that TRMT1 Gln530Lys was resistant to Mpro cleavage and did not observe the formation of cleavage products (e.g. TRMT1 MT domain) compared to cleavage of TRMT1 WT under the same proteolytic conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mouse or hamster TRMT1 is not cleaved by Mpro when these enzymes are co-expressed in cells.
source: This is consistent with a more recent report showing that mouse or hamster TRMT1 is not cleaved by Mpro when these enzymes are co-expressed in cells (Lu and Zhou, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu and Zhou, 2023.

claim: The TRMT1 Gln530Lys substitution at the invariant P1 glutamine residue is sufficient to completely prevent TRMT1 proteolysis in vitro.
source: Our results confirm that the TRMT1 Gln530Lys substitution at the invariant P1 glutamine residue is sufficient to completely prevent TRMT1 proteolysis in vitro, strongly suggesting this mutation would prevent SARS-CoV Mpro-directed TRMT1 cleavage during Muroidea infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The TRMT1 Gln530Lys mutation would likely prevent SARS-CoV Mpro-directed TRMT1 cleavage during Muroidea infection.
source: Our results confirm that the TRMT1 Gln530Lys substitution at the invariant P1 glutamine residue is sufficient to completely prevent TRMT1 proteolysis in vitro, strongly suggesting this mutation would prevent SARS-CoV Mpro-directed TRMT1 cleavage during Muroidea infection.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MD simulations show TRMT1 is stably bound to the Mpro active site and primarily adopts the P3′-in conformation observed in the crystal structure.
source: MD simulations show TRMT1 is stably bound to the Mpro active site and primarily adopts the P3′-in conformation observed in the crystal structure, where TRMT1 Phe533 occupies the S3′ pocket with a probability of ~65% over the course of the 100 ns simulation (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: TRMT1 Phe533 occupies the S3′ pocket with a probability of ~65% over the course of the 100 ns simulation.
source: MD simulations show TRMT1 is stably bound to the Mpro active site and primarily adopts the P3′-in conformation observed in the crystal structure, where TRMT1 Phe533 occupies the S3′ pocket with a probability of ~65% over the course of the 100 ns simulation (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Simulations of the nsp4/5-Mpro complex show the nsp4/5 peptide primarily adopts the P3′-out conformation, where nsp4/5 Phe531 is oriented away from the Mpro surface with ~70% probability.
source: In contrast, simulations of the nsp4/5-Mpro complex show the nsp4/5 peptide primarily adopts the P3′-out conformation, where nsp4/5 Phe531 is oriented away from the Mpro surface with ~70% probability, consistent with the observed nsp4/5 binding mode in the crystal structure.
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The dominant binding modes for TRMT1 and nsp4/5 peptide substrates (P3′-in vs -out, respectively) are consistent across the crystal structures and MD simulations.
source: This computational analysis shows that while P3′-in and -out conformations can interconvert, the dominant binding modes for TRMT1 and nsp4/5 peptide substrates (P3′-in vs -out, respectively) are consistent across the crystal structures and MD simulations.
evidence: Conclusion based on MD simulation and structural data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The computationally and experimentally determined substrate binding poses fail to explain the large differences in cleavage kinetics observed for TRMT1 vs nsp4/5.
source: Furthermore, because these conformations differ primarily at the C-terminal end of the peptide but have very similar geometries at the scissile amide bond, we find that the computationally and experimentally determined substrate binding poses fail to explain the large differences in cleavage kinetics observed for TRMT1 vs nsp4/5.
evidence: Inference based on structural and MD simulation data.

claim: The Mpro-nsp4/5 complex has only ~9% increased probability to fall within 89±7° nucleophilic attack angle, as compared with the Mpro-TRMT1 complex over the course of the simulation.
source: The distribution of the S–C=O nucleophilic attack angle shows that the Mpro-nsp4/5 complex has only ~9% increased probability to fall within 89±7°, as compared with the Mpro-TRMT1 complex over the course of the simulation (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The nsp4/5 peptide shows slightly more favorable positioning of Cys145 for nucleophilic attack in the Michaelis complex during the first step of cleavage, but this is not nearly sufficient to explain the large difference (~200-fold in kcat) in experimentally observed cleavage kinetics between nsp4/5 and TRMT1.
source: Thus, while the nsp4/5 peptide shows slightly more favorable positioning of Cys145 for nucleophilic attack in the Michaelis complex during the first step of cleavage, this is not nearly sufficient to explain the large difference (~200-fold in kcat) in experimentally observed cleavage kinetics between nsp4/5 and TRMT1.
evidence: Inference based on MD simulation and kinetic data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 5.

claim: Kinetic discrimination between peptide cleavage rates is likely to occur during a later step in the Mpro-catalyzed cleavage reaction that follows substrate binding, Michaelis complex formation, and initial nucleophilic attack.
source: Taken together with our TRMT1-Mpro structure and kinetic analysis of Mpro and TRMT1 mutants, these results strongly suggest that kinetic discrimination between peptide cleavage rates is likely to occur during a later step in the Mpro-catalyzed cleavage reaction that follows substrate binding, Michaelis complex formation, and initial nucleophilic attack, similar to some serine proteases (Radisky, 2002).
evidence: Inference based on structural, kinetic, and MD simulation data, with citation to Radisky, 2002.

claim: Recent studies mapping host-coronavirus protein interaction networks predicted high confidence interactions between the SARS-CoV-1 or SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro) and the human tRNA-modifying enzyme TRMT1.
source: Recent studies mapping host-coronavirus protein interaction networks predicted high confidence interactions between the SARS-CoV-1 or SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro) and the human tRNA-modifying enzyme TRMT1 (Gordon et al., 2020b; Meyer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon et al., 2020b; Meyer et al., 2021.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 Mpro can recognize and cleave the human TRMT1 526–536 sequence located between the TRMT1 methyltransferase and zinc finger domains.
source: In this work, we show that SARS-CoV-2 Mpro can recognize and cleave the human TRMT1 526–536 sequence located between the TRMT1 methyltransferase and zinc finger domains and that cleavage of TRMT1 impairs tRNA substrate binding and abolishes tRNA m2,2G modification activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Cleavage of TRMT1 impairs tRNA substrate binding and abolishes tRNA m2,2G modification activity.
source: In this work, we show that SARS-CoV-2 Mpro can recognize and cleave the human TRMT1 526–536 sequence located between the TRMT1 methyltransferase and zinc finger domains and that cleavage of TRMT1 impairs tRNA substrate binding and abolishes tRNA m2,2G modification activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Mpro is able to efficiently cleave the TRMT1 526–536 sequence in recombinant FL TRMT1, as well as in endogenous TRMT1 from human cell lysate.
source: Mpro is able to efficiently cleave the TRMT1 526–536 sequence in recombinant FL TRMT1, as well as in endogenous TRMT1 from human cell lysate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The kinetic parameters determined for Mpro-mediated TRMT1 (526–536) peptide proteolysis are very similar to those measured for the known nsp8/9 viral polypeptide cleavage site.
source: The kinetic parameters determined for Mpro-mediated TRMT1 (526–536) peptide proteolysis are very similar to those measured for the known nsp8/9 viral polypeptide cleavage site.
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The structure of human TRMT1 (526–536) in complex with SARS-CoV-2 Mpro C145A reveals a distinct binding mode for the TRMT1 substrate peptide that engages the Mpro S3′ pocket.
source: We also determined the structure of human TRMT1 (526–536) in complex with SARS-CoV-2 Mpro C145A, which reveals a distinct binding mode for the TRMT1 substrate peptide that engages the Mpro S3′ pocket.
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: TRMT1 526–536 is highly conserved in primates and mammals.
source: Finally, though TRMT1 526–536 is highly conserved in primates and mammals, we found that Muroidea contains a critical substitution which confers Mpro cleavage resistance.
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Muroidea contains a critical substitution which confers Mpro cleavage resistance.
source: Finally, though TRMT1 526–536 is highly conserved in primates and mammals, we found that Muroidea contains a critical substitution which confers Mpro cleavage resistance.
evidence: Supported by evolutionary analysis and experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Human TRMT1 is cleaved during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Importantly, and concurrent with our own work, Zhang et al., 2024, report that human TRMT1 is cleaved during SARS-CoV-2 infection and that this leads to loss of m2,2G modification in virally infected cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2024.

claim: Cleavage of human TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection leads to loss of m2,2G modification in virally infected cells.
source: Importantly, and concurrent with our own work, Zhang et al., 2024, report that human TRMT1 is cleaved during SARS-CoV-2 infection and that this leads to loss of m2,2G modification in virally infected cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2024.

claim: Viruses have evolved diverse strategies that subvert host protein synthesis in order to downregulate host translation and optimize the translation of viral proteins.
source: Viruses have evolved diverse strategies that subvert host protein synthesis in order to downregulate host translation and optimize the translation of viral proteins (de Breyne et al., 2020; Jan et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2012; Walsh and Mohr, 2011; Roberts et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (de Breyne et al., 2020; Jan et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2012; Walsh and Mohr, 2011; Roberts et al., 2009).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 employs multiple mechanisms to disrupt host protein synthesis.
source: SARS-CoV-2 employs multiple mechanisms to disrupt host protein synthesis (Thoms et al., 2020; Finkel et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021; Puray-Chavez et al., 2022; Eriani and Martin, 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Banerjee et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Thoms et al., 2020; Finkel et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021; Puray-Chavez et al., 2022; Eriani and Martin, 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Banerjee et al., 2020).

claim: Mpro-mediated cleavage of human TRMT1 could contribute to the modulation of cellular translation during viral infection.
source: SARS-CoV-2 employs multiple mechanisms to disrupt host protein synthesis (Thoms et al., 2020; Finkel et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021; Puray-Chavez et al., 2022; Eriani and Martin, 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Banerjee et al., 2020), and Mpro-mediated cleavage of human TRMT1 could contribute to the modulation of cellular translation during viral infection.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on experimental data and known functions of TRMT1.

claim: TRMT1 is a tRNA methyltransferase whose m2,2G26 modification activity directly impacts global translational efficiency.
source: TRMT1 is a tRNA methyltransferase whose m2,2G26 modification activity directly impacts global translational efficiency.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about TRMT1 function.

claim: Knockouts of TRMT1 result in loss of the m2,2G26 tRNA modification and a significant decrease in translation levels in HEK293T cells.
source: Knockouts of TRMT1, or truncations of TRMT1 that remove its zinc finger domain, result in loss of the m2,2G26 tRNA modification and a significant decrease in translation levels in HEK293T cells (Dewe et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dewe et al., 2017.

claim: Truncations of TRMT1 that remove its zinc finger domain result in loss of the m2,2G26 tRNA modification and a significant decrease in translation levels in HEK293T cells.
source: Knockouts of TRMT1, or truncations of TRMT1 that remove its zinc finger domain, result in loss of the m2,2G26 tRNA modification and a significant decrease in translation levels in HEK293T cells (Dewe et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dewe et al., 2017.

claim: TRMT1-deficient human cells exhibit increased sensitivity to oxidative stress.
source: Additionally, TRMT1-deficient human cells, or cells with inactivating TRMT1 truncations, exhibit increased sensitivity to oxidative stress and links to neurological dysfunction (Blaesius et al., 2018; Davarniya et al., 2015; Najmabadi et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Blaesius et al., 2018; Davarniya et al., 2015; Najmabadi et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2020a).

claim: Cells with inactivating TRMT1 truncations exhibit increased sensitivity to oxidative stress and links to neurological dysfunction.
source: Additionally, TRMT1-deficient human cells, or cells with inactivating TRMT1 truncations, exhibit increased sensitivity to oxidative stress and links to neurological dysfunction (Blaesius et al., 2018; Davarniya et al., 2015; Najmabadi et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Blaesius et al., 2018; Davarniya et al., 2015; Najmabadi et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2020a).

claim: Mpro-mediated cleavage of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection may contribute to the downregulation of host translation.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that Mpro-mediated cleavage of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection may contribute to the downregulation of host translation and oxidative stress-related pathogenesis and phenotypes (Cecchini and Cecchini, 2020).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on experimental data and citation to Cecchini and Cecchini, 2020.

claim: Mpro-mediated cleavage of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection may contribute to oxidative stress-related pathogenesis and phenotypes.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that Mpro-mediated cleavage of TRMT1 during SARS-CoV-2 infection may contribute to the downregulation of host translation and oxidative stress-related pathogenesis and phenotypes (Cecchini and Cecchini, 2020).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on experimental data and citation to Cecchini and Cecchini, 2020.

claim: The TRMT1 (526–536) cleavage sequence is found in a linker region between structured domains.
source: Indeed, although the TRMT1 (526–536) cleavage sequence is found in a linker region between structured domains, an AlphaFold2-predicted (Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021) TRMT1 structure suggests that many of these residues make contacts with the surface of the TRMT1 methyltransferase domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which may be important for enzyme stability, domain orientation, or function.
evidence: Supported by AlphaFold2 prediction cited from Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021, and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many residues in the TRMT1 (526–536) cleavage sequence make contacts with the surface of the TRMT1 methyltransferase domain.
source: Indeed, although the TRMT1 (526–536) cleavage sequence is found in a linker region between structured domains, an AlphaFold2-predicted (Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021) TRMT1 structure suggests that many of these residues make contacts with the surface of the TRMT1 methyltransferase domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which may be important for enzyme stability, domain orientation, or function.
evidence: Supported by AlphaFold2 prediction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Contacts between TRMT1 (526–536) residues and the TRMT1 methyltransferase domain may be important for enzyme stability, domain orientation, or function.
source: Indeed, although the TRMT1 (526–536) cleavage sequence is found in a linker region between structured domains, an AlphaFold2-predicted (Varadi et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021) TRMT1 structure suggests that many of these residues make contacts with the surface of the TRMT1 methyltransferase domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which may be important for enzyme stability, domain orientation, or function.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on AlphaFold2 prediction.

claim: The TRMT1-Mpro structure shows an uncommon peptide binding mode in which the P3′ TRMT1 Phe residue is buried in the S3′ pocket on the Mpro surface ('P3′-in' conformation).
source: First, our TRMT1-Mpro structure shows an uncommon peptide binding mode in which the P3′ TRMT1 Phe residue is buried in the S3′ pocket on the Mpro surface ('P3′-in' conformation; Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Of the currently known Mpro-peptide substrate structures, the unique Mpro P3′-in binding mode is only seen for TRMT1 and nsp6/7.
source: Of the currently known Mpro-peptide substrate structures, this unique Mpro P3′-in binding mode is only seen for TRMT1 and nsp6/7, though notably the P3′-in conformation has also been observed in a crystal structure of SARS-CoV-1 Mpro in complex with its C-terminal auto-processing site (VTFQGKFK), which like TRMT1, contains a phenylalanine at the P3′ site (Muramatsu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison and citation to Muramatsu et al., 2016.

claim: The P3′-in conformation has been observed in a crystal structure of SARS-CoV-1 Mpro in complex with its C-terminal auto-processing site (VTFQGKFK), which contains a phenylalanine at the P3′ site.
source: Of the currently known Mpro-peptide substrate structures, this unique Mpro P3′-in binding mode is only seen for TRMT1 and nsp6/7, though notably the P3′-in conformation has also been observed in a crystal structure of SARS-CoV-1 Mpro in complex with its C-terminal auto-processing site (VTFQGKFK), which like TRMT1, contains a phenylalanine at the P3′ site (Muramatsu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muramatsu et al., 2016.

claim: The unique binding mode demonstrates the flexible accommodation of diverse substrate binding poses in the Mpro active site.
source: This unique binding mode demonstrates the flexible accommodation of diverse substrate binding poses in the Mpro active site and highlights the availability of the S3′ pocket for inhibitor binding and therapeutic design.
evidence: Inference based on structural data.

claim: The unique binding mode highlights the availability of the S3′ pocket for inhibitor binding and therapeutic design.
source: This unique binding mode demonstrates the flexible accommodation of diverse substrate binding poses in the Mpro active site and highlights the availability of the S3′ pocket for inhibitor binding and therapeutic design.
evidence: Inference based on structural data.

claim: Mutations to residues on the surface of Mpro involved in direct binding and recognition of substrate, including Met49, Asn142, and Gln189, have surprisingly little impact on cleavage kinetics.
source: Second, consistent with previous mutagenesis studies of Mpro (Flynn et al., 2022), we find that mutations to residues on the surface of Mpro involved in direct binding and recognition of substrate, including Met49, Asn142, and Gln189, have surprisingly little impact on cleavage kinetics (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5D and citation to Flynn et al., 2022.

claim: Mutating TRMT1 P1′ Ala531 to Ser had no effect on cleavage kinetics.
source: Similarly, mutating TRMT1 P1′ Ala531 to Ser (the P1′ residue in nsp4/5 and most other substrate sequences) had no effect on cleavage kinetics and MD simulations still predict this peptide will favor the P3′-in binding conformation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MD simulations predict the TRMT1 A531S peptide will favor the P3′-in binding conformation.
source: Similarly, mutating TRMT1 P1′ Ala531 to Ser (the P1′ residue in nsp4/5 and most other substrate sequences) had no effect on cleavage kinetics and MD simulations still predict this peptide will favor the P3′-in binding conformation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by MD simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The scissile amide bond that links substrate residues P1 and P1′ are positioned almost identically in the active site in nsp4/5-, nsp8/9-, and TRMT1-bound Mpro crystal structures.
source: Third, comparing nsp4/5-, nsp8/9-, and TRMT1-bound Mpro crystal structures, the scissile amide bond that links substrate residues P1 and P1′ are positioned almost identically in the active site and located at similar distances from the Cys145Ala residue (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deviations away from 180° in the dihedral angle of the scissile amide bond in Mpro-peptide structures are inconsistent with the observed trends in peptide cleavage rates.
source: Likewise, deviations away from 180° in the dihedral angle of the scissile amide bond in these Mpro-peptide structures, which could indicate ground state destabilization and help explain accelerated proteolysis for nsp4/5 (Zhou et al., 2016), are also inconsistent with the observed trends in peptide cleavage rates (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and citation to Zhou et al., 2016.

claim: The large differences in catalytic efficiency observed for Mpro-mediated cleavage of nsp4/5 vs nsp8/9 and TRMT1 are not easily explained by structural analysis of the substrate-bound Mpro structures or the Mpro-peptide geometries and conformations observed in the MD simulations.
source: Therefore, the large differences in catalytic efficiency observed for Mpro-mediated cleavage of nsp4/5 vs nsp8/9 and TRMT1 are not easily explained by structural analysis of the substrate-bound Mpro structures or the Mpro-peptide geometries and conformations observed in the MD simulations.
evidence: Conclusion based on structural and MD simulation data.

claim: The conformational preferences of bound substrates are not clearly linked to simple sequence features.
source: Taken together, our structural, kinetic, and computational data described above suggest that: (a) the conformational preferences of bound substrates are not clearly linked to simple sequence features
evidence: Inference based on structural, kinetic, and computational data.

claim: Mutations to individual residues on Mpro or its peptide substrate that appear important for Mpro-substrate interactions or conformation are often insufficient to change binding conformation or cleavage kinetics.
source: Taken together, our structural, kinetic, and computational data described above suggest that: (a) the conformational preferences of bound substrates are not clearly linked to simple sequence features, (b) mutations to individual residues on Mpro or its peptide substrate that appear important for Mpro-substrate interactions or conformation are often insufficient to change binding conformation or cleavage kinetics
evidence: Inference based on structural, kinetic, and computational data.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 Mpro is vital for viral propagation and is thus a major target for antiviral drug development.
source: SARS-CoV-2 Mpro is vital for viral propagation and is thus a major target for antiviral drug development (Burkhardt et al., 2023; Cwilichowska et al., 2022; Katre et al., 2022; Steuten et al., 2021; Narayanan et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Burkhardt et al., 2023; Cwilichowska et al., 2022; Katre et al., 2022; Steuten et al., 2021; Narayanan et al., 2022).

claim: Consideration of the S3′ pocket on the Mpro surface could aid in the design of potent and specific SARS-CoV-2 Mpro inhibitors.
source: Consideration of the often-hidden S3′ pocket on the Mpro surface could aid in the design of potent and specific SARS-CoV-2 Mpro inhibitors.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on structural data.

claim: The vast majority of Mpro inhibitors target the S2 and S1 sites of Mpro, with peptidyl inhibitors designed with glutamine and leucine analogs for the P2 and P1 positions, respectively.
source: Currently, the vast majority of inhibitors target the S2 and S1 sites of Mpro, with peptidyl inhibitors designed with glutamine and leucine analogs for the P2 and P1 positions, respectively (Agost-Beltrán et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Agost-Beltrán et al., 2022.

claim: The flexible S3′ pocket could be utilized in future therapeutic design.
source: Our structural results suggest the flexible S3′ pocket could be utilized in future therapeutic design, and together with our kinetic analysis adds to the growing understanding of Mpro substrate recognition and cleavage efficiency that is critical for potent and specific targeting of Mpro to prevent or treat infection.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on structural data.
